O.outcome_detail: percent of family income required to pay for college after grant aid

cells.quote: Every year, this extraordinary financial burden requires low-income families to pay or borrow an amount equivalent to nearly three-quarters of their family income for just one child to attend a four-year college. In contrast, middle-class students must finance the equivalent of 27 percent of their family income to go to college, while high-income students must finance just 14 percent (Table 1).
cells.note: Education-cost comparison based on NPSAS:08 analysis; no instructional treatment was manipulated.

D.treatment: institutions with net price exceeding 100% of low-income family income

O.outcome_detail: net price for low-income students as a percent of average family income

cells.quote: In fact, 275 institutions require their lowest income students to pay more 100 percent of their annual family income to attend college (Figure 1).
cells.note: The study text contains the typographical wording “more 100 percent”; the intended comparison is institutions above versus below the 100-percent-income burden threshold.

D.treatment: five institutions meeting affordability, graduation, and low-income-enrollment criteria

O.outcome_detail: combined affordability, graduation rate, and low-income-student enrollment

cells.quote: Across the country, 1,186 four-year colleges and universities in America have comparable data on what low-income students actually pay to attend college. Of these, only five open their doors to a proportion of low-income students that is at or above the national average, provide all of their students with at least a 1-in-2 chance at graduating, and ask low-income students to pay a portion of their family income no greater than what the average middle-income student in the United States pays.
cells.note: The criteria were net price of $4,600 or less, graduation rate of at least 50 percent, and at least 30 percent Pell enrollment.

D.treatment: students from families in the top income quintile at private nonprofit institutions
D.comparison: students from families in the bottom income quintile at private nonprofit institutions

cells.quote: Private nonproﬁt colleges and universities spent almost twice as much on students from families in the top quintile of family income as they did on those in the bottom quintile.
cells.note: This is an observational comparison of institutional grant-aid distributions.

D.comparison: residencies not providing PS data to residents

cells.quote: This survey found that only 27% of responding residencies provide any PS data to their residents.
cells.note: The contrast is an observed survey prevalence, not an instructional intervention.

O.outcome_detail: provision of an organized PE curriculum

cells.quote: There was no significant difference in numbers of AOA and ACGME programs providing curicula (p=0.32).
cells.note: The study is a cross-sectional survey; no educational condition was assigned.
